$layer.anchor coordinate anchors

Reference named entity geometry inside coordinate arguments.

$face.x · $face.y $face.left · $face.top $face.centerX · $face.centerY $face.right · $face.bottom $face.width · $face.height $face.rotation · $face.zIndex $face.left+4 · $face.top-2 $last.width · $last.height

Type $ for variables or $last. for known properties.

If no previous entity exists, every $last anchor is 0.

sq 100 x-$last.width sq 50 x:$last.x+$last.width
math integer expressions

Use arithmetic on numbers, local variables, or layer anchors. Expressions cannot contain spaces.

+   -   *   /   %   ( ) sq 10+2 rect 20 $width/2 sq 64 x:$last.width-10 chradius button $radius+2 $smiley.rotation=0 $panel.x=$last.right+4

Writable properties: x, y, edges, centers, rotation, radius, and zIndex.

key:value named arguments

Use named arguments in any order, or place them after required positional arguments.

sq size:64 color:hotpink radius:8 id:button sq 64 x:-100 sq size:100 x:-$last.width rect height:40 width:80 x:20 y:30 id:panel move layer:panel x:10 y:-4 pixels color:black points:4,4;7,4 id:eyes

Proof of concept

Interfaces as executable functions

I made this as a proof of concept for another IDE and live-code style utility for generating XPM—or really anything that can be expressed through functions.

The idea is simple: interfaces should manipulate functions, and those functions should also be executable. Moving a layer, setting a color, or changing a property should have an equivalent command. A small set of commands becomes art. 

addcolor smileyellow #ffd84d
addcolor smileorange #f28c28
cir 12 smileyellow as face
cirstroke face 1 1 black as face-lines
pixels black 4,4 7,4 as eyes
pixels smileorange 4,6 7,6 5,7..6,7 as mouth
group face face-lines eyes mouth as smiley
becomes art
